text.content:
Everything the flock needs to know: who you are, how to roll, how to hide, and how to hold in a gobble when the farmer is close enough to tickle.

It’s Thanksgiving morning on the farm. The sun is up, the frost is melting off the pumpkins, and inside the farmhouse the farmer is pulling on his boots and humming. The oven is warming up. The family is coming at four. The farmer is looking for a turkey. Any turkey.

You are a turkey.

In Don’t Get Gobble Gobbled, each player is one turkey in a flock of friends. You can’t fight the farmer, and you can’t outrun him for long. What you can do is hide in the hayloft, sneak behind the cows, tip over the milk pails, let the goats loose and generally waste his entire morning, until it’s far too late to roast anybody. Then the family eats something else, and the flock struts off into the sunset.

There’s just one problem. You’re a turkey, and when turkeys get nervous, they gobble.

How you win

The Dinner Clock counts down toward Too Late: the moment it’s too late to cook a turkey in time for dinner. When it gets there, the farmer gives up, and the whole flock wins. Every round moves the clock on, and every prank you pull moves it on further.

How you lose

If the farmer grabs one turkey, the game ends at once. That turkey gets gobbled (this is a cartoon: it goes into the kitchen with a very surprised look on its face), and the whole flock loses, together. You could leave a slow friend behind to save your own feathers, but that’s not how turkeys roll, and it wouldn’t help: in this game, nobody wins alone.

Nobody is ever knocked out early, either. Everyone plays right to the end, because the end comes for all of you at once.

What kind of game is this?

A party game with a little roleplaying in it. Each player runs one turkey: what it does, what it says, and how loudly it gobbles. One more person is the Storyteller, who runs the farmer, the farm dog, the farmer’s kid and the farm itself by following simple tables (Part Two). The Storyteller isn’t playing against you; the dice and the tables decide what the farmer does. The Storyteller’s job is to make him loud, silly and just a little bit scary.

  • Players: 2 to 8 turkeys, plus the Storyteller.
  • Ages: 8 and up. Younger turkeys can play with a grown-up helping them read.
  • Time: about an hour with 2 turkeys, up to about 2 hours with 8, including 15 minutes of setup (Chapter 8 has the details).
  • One night only: every game is complete in itself. Play it again next year on a different farm.

What you need

  • Ten six-sided dice (d6): 3 white action dice, 5 red gobble dice, 1 helper die in any other color, and 1 die for the Storyteller (any color). Ordinary board-game dice are perfect.
  • Printed from this book: the map and farm table of the farm you’re playing (Chapters 9 to 11), a turkey card for each player, the Dinner Clock sheet, the tokens sheet, and the two reference sheets (At the Table, and the Storyteller’s Card).
  • Something to mark things with: a coin or paperclip for each turkey’s urge, a coin for the clock, and the cut-out tokens (or coins and buttons) for the turkeys, the farmer, the dog, the kid, the decoy, the Feathers and the “Huh?” tokens. Cut them out before game night.
  • A pencil, for ticking off pranks.

Chapter 12, Your First Night, walks through setting up and teaching the game.

The whole game in one breath

Every round, each turkey does one thing: sneak, hunker down, pull a prank, save a friend, or let out a gobble on purpose. Then the farmer walks, looks for turkeys, and maybe finds one. Rolls use white dice for what you’re trying to do and one red die for every point of your urge; any red 6 means you gobble, and a gobble tells the farmer where you are. If he spots you, your friends have one chance to save you before he grabs you. Get to Too Late with nobody grabbed, and you win.

The tone: slapstick

This is a comedy. The farmer trips over rakes. The goats get loose. A turkey hides inside a scarecrow and sneezes. When a turkey gets gobbled, it means dinner, but nothing in this book is ever gross or gory: being gobbled means a dramatic exit and some famous last words. Play it big, play it silly, and do the voices.

Party rules

Say it out loud

Whenever your turkey gobbles, you gobble too. Out loud. “GOBBLE GOBBLE!” Everyone else is allowed to gasp. This rule is always on.

Straight faces (optional)

Decide before you start whether to use this one. While the Storyteller is doing the farmer’s search (“Is there a turkey in the hayloft? Hmmm?”), turkeys are supposed to be very, very quiet. The first player to laugh out loud during a search raises their own turkey’s urge by 1. It only happens once per search, it never makes a turkey gobble at once (if its urge is already 5, it simply stays at 5), and it’s best for groups who enjoy being silly at each other. Skip it with very young players.

Turkey talk

  • A tom is a grown-up male turkey: big, puffed up, with a beard on his chest.
  • A hen is a female turkey: smaller than a tom, with no beard.
  • A jake is a young male, still growing into his gobble.
  • The floppy bit over the beak is the snood. It goes bright red when a turkey is excited. Today, it’s bright red a lot.

Designer’s Note

The best moments in this game happen when the farmer is right next to you, your urge is at 4, and you have to decide whether to stay perfectly still or make a run for it. Lean into those moments. Hold your breath. Look at the red dice. Then roll.

Eight turkeys live in the Turkey Pen, and every one of them has a plan for today, a talent, and at least one very bad habit. Each player plays one of them.

Choosing your turkey

Every turkey is ready to play: there’s nothing to build. Each has a knack (something it’s good at, usually an extra white die) and a quirk (a nervous habit that gets it into trouble). Every turkey is different, and there’s exactly one of each.

  • Pick: each player picks a turkey. If two players want the same one, they each roll a d6; the highest gets it (roll again on a tie), and the other picks again.
  • Or deal: shuffle the turkey cards and deal one to each player. This is quickest, and fun for a first game.
  • Or roll: the cards are numbered 1 to 8. Roll two dice: the first picks a half (1–3: cards 1 to 4; 4–6: cards 5 to 8), the second picks the card in it (roll again on a 5 or 6, or if that turkey is taken).

With fewer than eight players, the turkeys nobody picked stay in the pen, asleep, and aren’t part of the game. You can rename your turkey or draw your own version of it on the card; its knack and quirk stay the same.

Where a knack or quirk says something different from the general rules, the knack or quirk wins.

Butterbean

“Five minutes. Give me five minutes and that oven is off. Did I tell you about the oven?”

A Bourbon Red hen: chestnut feathers with white wings and a white tail. Butterbean is the busiest beak on the farm. If it can be pecked, unpicked, untied or unplugged, she’s already on it, and she’ll tell you all about it while she works. She never stops talking. Not even while hiding.

Knack: Busy Beak

+1 white die when you pull a Prank, and when the roll works it ticks two boxes.

Quirk: Chatterbox +1 urge after any roll where you Lend a Wing, or a friend Lends you one.

Play her: send Butterbean to the big pranks. Only Lend her a Wing (or ask for hers) when it really matters.

Pip

“I can be very quiet. Hic. Mostly.”

A Narragansett jake: steel-gray, black and tan, with barred wings. Pip is small, light on his feet and very good at tiptoeing. He has had the hiccups since Tuesday.

Knack: Soft Steps

+1 white die when you Sneak, and one Sneak can take you two zones (one roll covers both).

Quirk: Hiccups At the end of every round, roll one red die: on a 6 you gobble (hic!).

Play him: Pip gets to pranks fast. Keep him away from the farmer at the end of the round, when the hiccups come.

Duchess

“I am not hiding. I am posing. Behind a cabbage.”

A Royal Palm hen: snow-white, with crisp black edges on every feather. Duchess can stand so still that the farmer once hung his hat on her. But whenever she does something brilliant, she simply has to strike a pose about it.

Knack: Still as a Stump

+1 white die when you roll to stay hidden, and your red dice don’t count on those rolls.

Quirk: Show-off Whenever you roll a Great, you strike a pose: a “Huh?” token goes on your spot (or your zone, if you’re in the open). A pose struck while the farmer searches stays down after he clears his tokens, so he’ll be back.

Play her: Duchess can stay hidden almost anywhere, even right under the farmer’s nose. Keep her away from friends’ spots when she’s rolling for something flashy.

Big Tom

“OI! FARMER! OVER HERE! …Is he coming? He’s coming. Hide me.”

A Bronze tom: shiny copper feathers, a huge fan of a tail, and the loudest gobble in three counties. Big Tom is the flock’s bodyguard. He is also, secretly, terrified of the farmer. And the dog. And small mice.

Knack: Big Gobble

+1 white die when you Gobble for a Friend, and you can do it from two zones away (two paths).

Quirk: Scaredy A Close Call happens to you when the farmer or the dog ends in your zone or next to it.

Play him: stay within two zones of your friends, so you can bellow the farmer away when someone gets Spotted, but not right next door to him.

Noodle

“Can we go now? Now? How about now?”

A White Holland jake: all white, all legs and all go. Noodle is the fastest turkey on the farm and cannot sit still for one single second.

Knack: Quick Feet

+1 white die when you Scram, and a Scram that works can take you two zones (three on a Great).

Quirk: Restless You can’t Hunker Down two rounds in a row.

Play him: Noodle is the turkey most likely to get out of trouble. On the rounds he can’t sit still, a friend can Hunker Down for him, or he can let it out somewhere far from the farmer.

Clementine

“Breathe in. Breathe out. And please don’t stand on my tail feathers.”

A Blue Slate hen: soft blue-gray from beak to tail. Clementine does turkey yoga every morning and can calm anyone down, as long as they keep out of her personal space.

Knack: Cool Head

Hunker Down lowers your urge, or a friend’s, by 3 instead of 2.

Quirk: Fussy +1 urge whenever you end an action sharing a hiding spot, or another turkey squeezes into yours.

Play her: park Clementine in the same zone as the twitchiest turkey, but not in the same hiding spot.

Gizmo

“Has everyone had a snack? Is everyone warm? Where’s Pip? WHERE’S PIP?”

A Black Spanish tom: glossy black feathers with a green shine. Gizmo is a big soft tom who looks after the whole flock like a mother hen, and he frets terribly whenever anyone is in trouble.

Knack: Mother Hen

When you Hunker Down, every other turkey in your zone lowers its urge by 1 too.

(A friend you calm with that Hunker Down gets the usual −2, not −3.)

Quirk: Worrywart +1 urge whenever another turkey is Spotted.

Play him: Gizmo is best in the middle of a crowd: one Hunker Down calms everybody.

Hazel

“He’s going to the barn. I know because I watched him. WHO GOBBLED?”

A Chocolate hen: rich brown feathers, wide eyes, and a habit of peeking over things. Hazel always knows where the farmer is. She jumps out of her feathers at every gobble, though.

Knack: Keen Eye

At the start of the turkeys’ turn, the Storyteller rolls the farmer’s route die and tells the flock where he’ll walk if nothing else (a detour, a rake or a “Huh?” token) decides it. Close Calls don’t raise the urge of turkeys in your zone.

Quirk: Jumpy +1 urge whenever another turkey gobbles.

Play her: listen to Hazel. Then move.

pages.name: Chapter 3 — A Round on the Farm

text.content:
The game is played in rounds. In each round every turkey gets one go, then the farmer gets his, then the clock ticks on. Repeat until somebody gets grabbed or it’s Too Late.

The round

  1. The turkeys’ turn. Every turkey takes one action (below), in any order the flock likes. Talk it over: whoever is doing something risky usually goes first, so friends can help if it goes wrong. Each player decides what their own turkey does, and once a turkey has acted, it’s done for this turn.
  2. The farmer’s turn. The Storyteller moves the farmer, the dog and (in a big flock) the farmer’s kid, and they look for turkeys (Chapter 7). In round 1 the farmer is still indoors pulling on his boots, and there is no farmer’s turn at all. For the whole of round 1, he, the dog and the kid don’t count for anything: no Sneak needs a roll because of them, and nobody can be Spotted. Nobody may go into the Farmhouse in round 1, either. That’s your head start: scatter!
  3. The end of the round. The Dinner Clock moves down one space (Chapter 6); if that makes it Too Late, the flock wins and nothing else happens. If it lands on an EVENT space, the Storyteller rolls the farm event now. Then every turkey that isn’t Spotted raises its urge by 1 (Chapter 4), and Pip rolls for his hiccups.

The roll

Many actions need a roll. Every roll works the same way.

  • Take 1 white die. That’s your action die: it says whether you pull it off.
  • Take one red die for every point of your urge. At urge 0 you roll no red dice at all; at urge 5, five. These are your gobble dice.
  • Roll them all together.

Read the white dice. Every roll has a target, written like 4+. If your highest white die is at or above the target, it works; if not, it fails. Any white 6 is a Great: it works, and some actions give you a little extra.

Read the red dice. If any red die shows a 6, you gobble. It’s one gobble however many 6s there are. Chapter 4 says what a gobble does (nothing good).

The result comes first. Do what the white dice say (move, hide, tick a box), then deal with the gobble. If you sneak into the barn and gobble, you’re in the barn, gobbling.

There are no rolls against the farmer and no rolls to beat each other. The target is the only number that matters, and it never changes in the middle of a roll.

Boosts

A boost adds one white die to a roll. Roll all the white dice and use the highest. A roll never has more than 3 white dice, however many boosts you could get. There are three kinds:

Your knack

Most knacks give +1 white die on one kind of roll (Chapter 2).

Lend a Wing

A friend in the same zone as you can Lend a Wing on your roll: you add a white die, and your friend rolls the helper die (the one in the third color) along with yours. If the helper die shows a 6, your friend gobbles, not you. Lending a Wing doesn’t use your friend’s action (they can do it before or after their own go, and on rolls during the farmer’s turn), but:

  • only one friend can Lend a Wing on any one roll;
  • if your dice and the helper die both show a 6, you both gobble: that’s two gobbles, and it takes two Feathers to cancel them;
  • a friend who Lends a Wing during the farmer’s search is in his zone, so a 6 on the helper die makes the friend Spotted;
  • each turkey can Lend a Wing only once per round (turn your card sideways to remember);
  • a Spotted turkey can’t Lend a Wing.

Puff Up

Before you roll, you can Puff Up: raise your own urge by 1, and add a white die. Your new urge counts for this roll (one more red die), and it stays raised afterwards. You can’t Puff Up at urge 5, and you can’t Puff Up when you Gobble for a Friend.

Example: a roll

Pip is in the Big Barn with urge 2. Farmer Bramble is in the Cow Pasture, which is next to the Cornfield. Pip wants to Sneak to the Cornfield. The farmer is next to the zone Pip is entering, so it’s a roll, target 4+.

Pip’s knack, Soft Steps, gives him a second white die. He Puffs Up too (urge 2 to 3) for a third. He rolls 3 white dice and 3 red dice: white 2, 4, 1, red 3, 6, 1. His best white die is a 4: it works. He creeps into the Cornfield and hides in the Corn rows. But there’s a red 6: “Gobble… gobble?”

A “Huh?” token goes on the Corn rows, and Pip’s urge drops to 0. The flock could spend a Feather to cancel the gobble, but they decide not to: the farmer is coming this way anyway, and with urge 0 Pip will roll no red dice at all when he checks the Corn rows. Feathers are best saved for gobbles in the farmer’s own zone, which would make a turkey Spotted on the spot.

Actions

On the turkeys’ turn, each turkey does one of these. A Spotted turkey can only Scram.

Sneak

Move along a path to a zone next to yours. If a hiding spot there has room, you hide in it (you pick which); if not, you’re in the open.

  • Roll 4+ if the farmer is in or next to the zone you leave or the zone you enter. (“Next to” always means joined by a path.)
  • Otherwise roll 3+ if the zone you enter is Noisy (hens, ducks, sheep: they make a fuss).
  • Otherwise there’s nothing to roll: you just go.
  • If it fails, you still get there (and can still hide), but you’re noticed: if the farmer is in the zone you end in, you’re Spotted; otherwise put a “Huh?” token on your hiding spot, or on the zone if you’re in the open.
  • Great: you can keep going one more zone, if that move wouldn’t need a roll of its own.
  • Two zones at once (Pip’s Soft Steps): check every zone you leave or enter, the middle one too, and use the highest target. You can’t pass through the farmer’s zone. A Great still adds one more zone.

Hunker Down

Stay where you are and take some deep breaths. If you’re in the open and a spot in your zone has room, you hide in it first; if the farmer is in your zone, that takes a 4+ roll, and if it fails you’re Spotted. Then, whether or not you managed to hide, lower your urge by 2, or lower the urge of a friend in your zone by 2 instead. Urge never goes below 0.

You can’t move from one hiding spot to another in the same zone: to change spots, Sneak out.

When you Hunker Down, tell everyone how your turkey calms down. Counting feathers? Humming? A tiny bit of turkey yoga?

Pull a Prank

You must be in the zone where the prank is, and the farmer must not be. Roll; you need the prank’s target. If it works, tick one of its boxes; a Great ticks two. When all of a prank’s boxes are ticked, it happens (Chapter 6), and it’s done for the rest of the game. You stay where you are, hidden or not. Ticked boxes stay ticked, so friends can finish a prank you started.

Gobble for a Friend

The bravest thing a turkey can do. Pick a Spotted friend in your zone or a zone next to it, and gobble on purpose, as loudly as you can, so the farmer looks at you instead. Each Spotted turkey can be helped this way only once per round. If the rescuer ends up Spotted, that’s a new Spotted turkey, and another friend can try for it.

  • Your urge goes to 0. You roll no red dice and can’t Puff Up, but your knack and a friend’s Wing still count.
  • Roll 4+. If it works, your friend is no longer Spotted (it stays where it is).
  • Either way, the farmer turns toward you: if he’s in your zone, now you are Spotted; otherwise a “Huh?” token goes on your spot.
  • Great: he can’t tell where the gobble came from. No token, and you aren’t Spotted.

Scram

Only a Spotted turkey can Scram, and it’s the only thing a Spotted turkey can do. Roll 4+ (5+ on Hard). If it works, run along a path to a zone next door, hide in a spot there if one has room, and you’re no longer Spotted. A Great lets you keep running one more zone. If it fails, you’re still Spotted, and your friends had better help.

Let It Out

Sometimes you just have to. Gobble on purpose: your urge goes to 0, and a “Huh?” token goes on your spot (or your zone, if you’re in the open). The farmer will come and look. Do it where he’s far away, or do it to pull him away from your friends. Don’t do it in the same zone as him: that makes you Spotted.

“The trick is not to think about gobbling.” “Now I’m thinking about gobbling.” “GOBBLE.”

Every turkey has an urge to gobble. It builds up all morning, and it gets much worse when the farmer is close. Too much urge, and a gobble slips out and tells him exactly where you are.

Your urge

Your urge is a number from 0 to 5, kept on your turkey card. Every turkey starts the game at urge 1 (it’s Thanksgiving, after all). Your urge is how many red dice you roll (Chapter 3), so the higher it is, the more likely each roll is to end in a gobble.

UrgeRed diceChance a roll gobbles
00none
111 in 6
22about 3 in 10
33about 2 in 5
44about 1 in 2
55about 3 in 5

When your urge rises

Your urge goes up by 1:

  • at the end of every round, unless you’re Spotted (you have bigger things to worry about);
  • at a Close Call: when the farmer, or the dog, ends his turn in your zone and you aren’t Spotted (Chapter 5);
  • when you Puff Up for an extra white die (Chapter 3);
  • when your quirk says so;
  • when a farm event says so (Chapter 7).

One thing, one rise

Apart from Puffing Up and farm events, your urge rises at most once per action (yours or anyone’s), once per farmer’s turn and once at the end of each round, however many reasons there are. If the farmer and the dog both end up in your zone, that’s still one Close Call and +1. A farm event is its own thing: a backfiring truck raises everyone’s urge even if it just rose for something else.

A full urge

Your urge can’t go above 5. If it’s at 5 and something would raise it, you gobble instead, and it goes back to 0. A full-urge gobble can’t be stopped with a Feather. Watch out: at urge 5 in the farmer’s zone, the Close Call at the end of his search makes you gobble, and that means Spotted. Hunker Down before you get there.

Calming down

The only way to lower your urge, apart from gobbling, is to Hunker Down (−2, Chapter 3), have a friend Hunker Down for you, or get lucky with a farm event. Urge never goes below 0.

Gobbling

However it happens, a gobble always does the same three things:

  1. Say it out loud. “GOBBLE GOBBLE!” (This is a rule.)
  2. Your urge goes to 0. Ahhh. That’s better.
  3. The farmer hears it. If he’s in your zone, you’re Spotted (Chapter 5). If he isn’t, put a “Huh?” token on your hiding spot, or on your zone if you’re in the open. He’ll come and have a look.

If a friend gobbles because of the helper die when Lending you a Wing, it’s your friend who gobbles, from your friend’s own spot.

Gobbling on purpose

Two actions are gobbles on purpose: Let It Out and Gobble for a Friend (Chapter 3). They work like any other gobble, except that Gobble for a Friend has its own rules about whom the farmer looks at.

Feathers

The flock shares a little pile of Feathers. A Feather is a friend’s wing clapped over your beak just in time.

  • After any roll, if a red die (or the helper die) shows a 6, the flock can spend one Feather to cancel that gobble. Nobody gobbles, no token goes down, and the urge stays where it is.
  • One Feather cancels one gobble. Feathers don’t come back once they’re spent.
  • A Feather can’t stop a gobble on purpose or a full-urge gobble. It can stop one of Pip’s hiccups, which come from a die.
  • The flock usually starts with 2 Feathers: Chapter 8 has the exact number for your flock size and difficulty.

Decide together whether to spend one. A gobble in the farmer’s own zone, which would make you Spotted, is nearly always worth a Feather. A gobble anywhere else resets your urge and sends him looking, and often that’s fine.

Example: near and far

Clementine is Pulling a Prank in the Duck Pond with urge 2, and the farmer is far away in the Farmhouse. Her roll gobbles. The flock keeps its Feathers: Clementine’s urge drops to 0, a “Huh?” token goes on the Reeds, and the farmer will start walking that way. That gives her a turn or two to move on.

Later, Noodle is hiding in the Hayloft when the farmer walks into the Big Barn and checks it. Noodle’s white dice say he stays hidden, but there’s a red 6. A gobble with the farmer in his zone means Spotted, so the flock spends a Feather straight away.

Designer’s Note

A gobble far from the farmer isn’t a disaster: it lets the steam out, and it can even pull him away from your friends. A gobble next to him is a disaster. Keep your urge low before you go anywhere near him, and Hunker Down before you have to.

The farm is a big game of hide-and-seek, and the farmer is “it”. This chapter is about where you can hide, how he finds you, and what happens when he does.

The farm map

Each farm (Chapters 9 to 11) is split into twelve zones: the Big Barn, the Duck Pond, the Turkey Pen and so on. Your turkey is always in exactly one zone. Zones are joined by paths, shown on the map as orange gaps in the fence; you can only Sneak along a path. No path, no way through (that’s a fence, a creek or a very grumpy goose). Two zones are next to each other only when a path joins them.

  • Hiding spots. Most zones have a few places to hide: the Hayloft, the Corn rows, behind the cows. Each spot shows its cover, the roll you need to stay hidden when it’s searched (3+ is safe, 5+ is risky), and its room, how many turkeys fit (×4 means four).
  • Hidden or in the open. A turkey in a hiding spot is hidden. A turkey that isn’t (no room, or nowhere to hide) is in the open. Turkeys can share a spot until it’s full.
  • Open zones have no hiding spots at all: anyone there is in the open.
  • Noisy zones are full of hens, ducks, goats, sheep or pigs who make a fuss: Sneaking into one takes a 3+ roll even when the farmer is far away (Chapter 3).

Everyone looks at the map. The tables under each map (the farmer’s route and search lines) are for the Storyteller. They aren’t secret, but the farmer is funnier when he’s a surprise.

How the farmer looks for you

On his turn, the farmer walks, then searches the zone he ends in (the Storyteller has the exact steps in Chapter 7).

  • If a “Huh?” token is down somewhere, he heads for the nearest one, up to two zones a turn, and checks the spot it’s on.
  • If not, he wanders along his route and checks one hiding spot, chosen by a die roll.
  • When he searches, everyone in the open in the zone he ends in is Spotted. He doesn’t spot anyone in zones he only walks through.
  • Every turkey in a spot he checks rolls to stay hidden: the target is the spot’s cover. If the roll fails, or gobbles, that turkey is Spotted.
  • Turkeys in the zone that he didn’t find still have a Close Call: +1 urge.

Your chance to stay hidden

With one white die and no boosts. A boost helps a lot; so does a low urge.

CoverUrge 012345
3+67%56%46%39%32%27%
4+50%42%35%29%24%20%
5+33%28%23%19%16%13%

“Huh?” tokens

A “Huh?” token is the farmer stopping, cupping a hand to his ear, and saying “Huh? What was that?”. It goes down when:

  • a turkey gobbles where the farmer isn’t (on its spot, or its zone if it’s in the open);
  • a Sneak fails (on the spot the sneaky turkey ends up in);
  • a turkey Gobbles for a Friend or Lets It Out (on its own spot);
  • the dog sniffs out a turkey, or the kid spots one (Chapter 7);
  • a loud prank goes off (on the prank’s zone, Chapter 6);
  • Duchess strikes a pose (her Show-off quirk, Chapter 2).

Tokens stay down until the farmer ends his turn in their zone and searches it. Then they all come off (except a pose Duchess strikes during that search). A turkey that Sneaks away from its token leaves the token behind, and the farmer will search an empty spot. That’s the idea.

The dog and the kid

On Standard and Hard, the farm dog wanders the farm and sometimes follows its nose toward the nearest turkey. It never grabs anyone, but if it ends its move in your zone you roll 4+ to stay hidden (it doesn’t care how good your spot is), and if you fail, it barks: a “Huh?” token on your spot. The dog gives you a Close Call too. The dog itself never makes anyone Spotted, but a gobble on its roll is an ordinary gobble: if the farmer is in your zone too, you’re Spotted.

With five or more turkeys, the farmer’s kid comes out to help Dad. The kid wanders, peeks into one hiding spot, and yells “DAD! TURKEY!” at any turkey it finds or sees in the open. That’s a “Huh?” token, not Spotted: the kid can’t grab you either.

Spotted!

Being Spotted means the farmer has seen you, and he’s coming. Turn your turkey token face down.

  • At the start of the farmer’s next turn, he grabs a Spotted turkey in his zone, and the game ends (below). If several are Spotted there, he grabs the one with the highest urge; on a tie, the Storyteller rolls a die to pick.
  • Until then, the flock has one chance to save you: the rest of the turkeys’ turn, if you were Spotted during it, or the whole next turkeys’ turn if you were Spotted on his turn or at the end of the round.
  • A Spotted turkey’s only action is Scram (Chapter 3). A Spotted turkey can’t Lend a Wing, and its urge doesn’t rise at the end of the round.
  • Friends can Gobble for a Friend (Chapter 3), once for each Spotted turkey each round.
  • You stop being Spotted when a Scram works, when a friend’s Gobble for a Friend works, or when the farmer isn’t in your zone at the start of his turn (Grandma called him away, or he carried off the decoy): he’s lost sight of you.

Grabbed

When the farmer grabs a turkey, the game ends at once and the whole flock loses. That turkey is gobbled: carried off to the kitchen, tucked under one arm, protesting loudly. Its player gets the last word (below). The only thing that can stop a grab is a decoy (Chapter 6).

Example: saving Duchess

Farmer Bramble wanders into the Big Barn and the Storyteller rolls his search line: the Hayloft. Duchess is in the Hayloft. She rolls to stay hidden, target 3+, with 2 white dice thanks to Still as a Stump (and her red dice don’t count): 1, 2. Spotted!

Next turkeys’ turn, Duchess tries to Scram first. Her urge is 1, so she Puffs Up (urge 2) for a second white die and rolls 2 white and 2 red: white 2, 3, red 4, 1. Still Spotted. Big Tom is next door in the Chicken Coop. He takes a deep breath and Gobbles for a Friend: his urge goes to 0, and he rolls 2 white dice (Big Gobble): 4, 6. A Great! The farmer spins round, can’t tell where that enormous gobble came from, and Duchess is no longer Spotted. Big Tom gets no “Huh?” token at all.

The farmer is still in the barn, though. Duchess should Sneak away next round, and she’ll need to roll for it.

Famous last gobbles

When a turkey gets grabbed, its player rolls a d6 (or makes up something better) for its last words as it’s carried off to the kitchen:

d6Last words
1“Tell my feathers I loved them.”
2“I regret NOTHING. Except the gobbling.”
3“Someone tell Grandma I said hi.”
4“Remember me as I was: hiding very, very badly.”
5“I’ll be back! Next Thanksgiving. Probably.”
6“GOBBLE GOBBLE!” (One last time, for the fans.)

pages.name: Chapter 6 — Pranks and the Dinner Clock

text.content:
A turkey needs hours in the oven, and the family arrives at four. Every minute the farmer spends chasing goats, mopping up milk or looking for his hat is a minute closer to Too Late. Your job is to waste as many of his minutes as you can.

The Dinner Clock

The Dinner Clock is a countdown track on the Dinner Clock sheet. At the start of the game, put a coin on the space Chapter 8 gives you (with four turkeys on Standard at Bramble Farm, that’s 20).

  • At the end of every round, it moves down 1 space.
  • When a prank happens, it moves down by the prank’s number, straight away.
  • When it reaches 0, it’s Too Late. The farmer looks at his watch, throws his hat on the ground, and gives up. The flock wins at once, even in the middle of a turn, and even if somebody is Spotted.

Farm events

Every space that’s a multiple of 4 (24, 20, 16, 12, 8 and 4) is an EVENT space. Whenever the coin lands on one, or jumps past one, the Storyteller rolls a farm event (Chapter 7): a backfiring truck, a phone call from Grandma, a rake in the grass. Jump past two at once and there are two events, in order. Putting the coin on its starting space doesn’t count, even if that’s an EVENT space. If a prank moves the clock, roll its events before dealing with that roll’s gobble.

Pranks

Every farm has eight pranks, one in each of eight zones, shown with a star on the map. Each one lists:

  • its target, the roll you need to Pull the Prank (Chapter 3);
  • its boxes: how many times the roll has to work (a Great ticks two);
  • its clock number: how far the Dinner Clock moves when it happens;
  • anything else it does: loud, detour or decoy.

You can’t pull a prank while the farmer is in its zone. When the last box is ticked, the prank happens: move the clock, then do whatever else it says. Each prank happens only once; after that it’s done for the game. When every prank is done, the clock still ticks down by itself every round.

Loud

It makes a terrible racket. Put a “Huh?” token on the prank’s zone (not on a spot: when the farmer gets there, he rolls for which spot to check). Pull it, then get out of there.

Detour

It gives the farmer something urgent to deal with. On his next turn he doesn’t walk the paths: he goes straight to the prank’s zone and spends his turn there being busy (rounding up cows, chasing a rowboat). He doesn’t search, but turkeys there still have a Close Call, and any “Huh?” tokens in that zone come off. The dog and the kid carry on as normal. If two detours go off before his turn, he goes to the one that went off first; the other waits for the turn after.

Decoy

Each farm has one decoy: a scarecrow, a hay bale or a pumpkin, dressed up as a turkey. When it happens, tick Decoy ready on the Dinner Clock sheet. The next time the farmer would grab a turkey, he grabs the decoy instead: that turkey isn’t Spotted any more, he carries the decoy all the way to the Farmhouse (put him there), the clock moves down 2, and he skips the rest of his own turn (no walking, searching or Close Calls). The dog and the kid still take theirs. Then the decoy is gone.

Example: turning off the oven

The Dinner Clock is at 14. Butterbean is in the Farmhouse, and the farmer is far away in the Cornfield. She Pulls a Prank: Turn off the oven, target 5+, two boxes, clock −3. Her urge is 1, so she rolls 2 white dice (Busy Beak) and 1 red: white 5, 2, red 3. It works, and Busy Beak makes the success count twice, so both boxes are ticked at once. The oven goes cold.

The clock jumps from 14 to 11. It passes the EVENT space on 12, so the Storyteller rolls a farm event.

Designer’s Note

A flock that only hides will usually be found in the end: the clock is long, and every round the farmer looks somewhere new. Pranks are risky, but they’re how you get to Too Late before he gets to you. The bigger your flock, the more you need them. Send your calmest turkeys, and keep everyone else out of the farmer’s way.

Too Late!

When the clock reaches 0, the farmer trudges back to the house, the family arrives, and someone has to make dinner out of whatever’s in the cupboard. The Storyteller rolls a d6 to see what they eat instead, while the flock does a victory strut:

d6What’s for dinner instead?
1Pizza, from the only place still open.
2Grandma’s famous tuna casserole. Nobody is sure about the crackers on top.
3A mountain of mashed potatoes, with lakes of gravy.
4Grilled cheese sandwiches for twenty-two.
5Breakfast for dinner: a tower of pancakes.
6The vegetable “turkey”: a cauliflower in a little paper hat.

Then the turkeys get the last word: each player says what their turkey does to celebrate.
